item.title: Awa Odori Dance Lesson: Learn the Steps — Guide
item.description: You don’t need to come during the August festival to experience Awa Odori — at the Awa Odori Kaikan in Tokushima city, the dance is celebrated all year round. The hall stages regular live performances by professional ‘ren’ dance troupes, who demonstrate the men’s dynamic low crouch and the women’s elegant, poised style to live drums and shamisen. Best of all, at the end audience members are invited up to learn and try the steps themselves in a fun, hands-on lesson, guided by the dancers — a great way to feel the rhythm and joy of Awa Odori firsthand.

item.title: Bizen Pottery Making Workshop: Throw Your Own — Guide
item.description: Making Bizen ware yourself is one of the most satisfying craft experiences in Okayama, precisely because the result is out of your hands. Studios around Imbe run classes in which you shape a cup, bowl or small vase either by hand-building or on the potter’s wheel, guided by a working potter. Because Bizen uses no glaze, what happens next is decided entirely by the kiln: your piece is fired for days in a wood-burning kiln alongside the studio’s own work, and the ash, flame and smoke give it colours and marks nobody can predict.

item.title: Calligraphy in Kyoto: A Shodo Brush Experience — Guide
item.description: Shodo, the way of writing, is one of Japan’s most revered arts, and a calligraphy experience in Kyoto is a quiet, meditative counterpoint to sightseeing. Guided by a teacher in a studio, machiya or temple, you begin by grinding an ink stick against a stone with water — a slow ritual that settles the mind — before learning to hold the brush and form the strokes of a character in the correct order and rhythm.

item.title: Fugu Preparation Class in Shimonoseki — Guide
item.description: Because fugu can be lethal if prepared wrongly, only chefs with a special licence earned through rigorous training and examination may handle and serve it — and in Shimonoseki, the heart of Japan’s fugu trade, some venues let curious visitors get a hands-on glimpse of that craft. A fugu preparation experience typically involves watching or trying, under close expert supervision, how the fish is cleaned, how its toxic parts are carefully removed and set aside, and how the flesh is sliced into the famous wafer-thin sashimi — before, of course, eating the results.

item.title: Hakata Ramen School: Make Your Own Ramen — Guide
item.description: For ramen lovers, a Hakata ramen-making class is a fun, hands-on way to get behind the counter of Fukuoka’s most famous dish. Guided by instructors, hands-on experiences let you learn the secrets of tonkotsu ramen — understanding the rich pork-bone broth, preparing the thin Hakata-style noodles, assembling the toppings, and finally cooking and eating a bowl of ramen you made yourself. Some classes are aimed at serious enthusiasts wanting to learn techniques in depth, others are casual, family-friendly experiences; either way you come away with real insight into what makes Hakata ramen special, and the satisfaction of eating your own creation.

item.title: Hakata-ori Silk Weaving Experience — Guide
item.description: Hakata-ori is Fukuoka’s celebrated traditional silk textile, woven in Hakata for over 770 years and prized above all for its firm, densely woven obi (kimono sashes), which produce a distinctive squeak when tied and hold a knot beautifully. Using many fine warp threads packed tightly together, the technique creates crisp geometric patterns, the most classic being the ‘kenjo’ design derived from Buddhist ritual implements. Once presented to the shogunate, Hakata-ori remains a proud symbol of the city’s craftsmanship.

item.title: Hiroshima Okonomiyaki Cooking Class: Build Your Own — Guide
item.description: Hiroshima okonomiyaki looks simple and is deceptively hard: the layering, the timing and above all the flip of a tall, loose stack take real skill, which is exactly what makes a cooking class here so satisfying. In a small group around a teppan griddle, an instructor walks you through spreading the thin crepe, piling on the cabbage and pork, steaming it down, frying the noodles alongside and finally combining and flipping the whole thing without collapse, before finishing with sauce, seaweed and bonito flakes.

item.title: Katsuo Tataki Cooking Class in Kochi — Guide
item.description: One of the most memorable food experiences in Kochi is searing your own katsuo tataki over a blazing straw fire. Hands-on classes and ‘warayaki’ (straw-grilling) experiences let visitors skewer a side of bonito and hold it over towering flames of burning rice straw, watching the surface char and smoke in dramatic fashion before it is sliced and dressed. It’s part cooking lesson, part spectacle — the flames leap impressively high — and the reward is eating tataki you seared yourself, fresher and more satisfying for the effort.

item.title: Kimono Rental in Asakusa — Guide
item.description: Renting a kimono in Asakusa is one of Tokyo’s most popular and enjoyable cultural experiences, letting you explore the atmospheric old-town streets around Senso-ji Temple dressed in beautiful traditional attire. Numerous rental shops cluster around Asakusa, offering a huge range of kimono (and yukata in summer) for men, women and children, with plans that typically include help getting dressed by staff, coordinated obi sashes and accessories, and often hair styling for an extra fee.

item.title: Osaka Okonomiyaki Cooking Class: Grill Your Own — Guide
item.description: Okonomiyaki, the hearty savoury pancake of cabbage, batter and toppings grilled on a hot iron plate, is Osaka’s defining home-style dish, and a cooking class is one of the most enjoyable ways to get under the skin of the city’s food culture. In a small group around a teppan, an instructor walks you through mixing the batter, grilling and the all-important flip, then eating what you’ve made hot off the plate, usually finished with sauce, mayonnaise, bonito flakes and seaweed.

item.title: Sake Tasting in Tokyo — Guide
item.description: Sake (nihonshu), Japan’s traditional rice wine, is central to the country’s culture and cuisine, and Tokyo is a superb place to explore it. The city is home to specialist sake bars, tasting rooms, standing bars (kaku-uchi) and shops offering flights and tastings that let you sample a range of premium sake from breweries across Japan — from crisp, dry styles to fruity, aromatic ginjo and daiginjo, unpasteurised nama, sparkling and aged varieties.

item.title: Sanuki Udon Making Workshop — Guide
item.description: For a fun, hands-on taste of Kagawa’s udon culture, join a Sanuki udon making workshop. Guided by instructors, you mix wheat flour, salt and water into a dough, then knead it to develop the signature springy ‘koshi’ texture — often by treading on it with your feet (wrapped in plastic), the traditional method, sometimes to music. You then roll the dough flat, fold and cut it into noodles, boil them and eat your own freshly made udon, usually with dashi broth and toppings.

item.title: Tea Ceremony Experience — Guide
item.description: A Japanese tea ceremony (chado or sado, ‘the way of tea’) is a refined, meditative ritual centred on the preparation and serving of matcha (powdered green tea), and taking part in one is a wonderful way to experience the depth and mindfulness of Japanese culture. Across Tokyo, tea houses, cultural centres and specialist studios offer tea ceremony experiences designed for visitors, many with English-speaking hosts. In a tranquil tatami room, a kimono-clad host demonstrates the graceful, precise movements of preparing the tea, explaining the etiquette, philosophy and seasonal aesthetics behind each gesture — the emphasis on harmony, respect, purity and tranquillity.

item.title: Wagashi Making Class in Kyoto: Shape Your Own Sweets — Guide
item.description: A wagashi-making class is one of the most rewarding hands-on experiences in Kyoto, a direct way into the city’s refined sweet-making tradition. Under the guidance of a confectioner, you learn to shape nerikiri — a smooth, pliable dough of sweet white-bean paste — by hand and with simple tools into the seasonal flowers, leaves and motifs that define kyo-wagashi. It is finer and more meditative work than it looks, demanding a gentle touch, and at the end you sit and eat the two or three sweets you have made with a bowl of matcha.

item.title: Zen Meditation in Kyoto: A Zazen Experience — Guide
item.description: As the historic centre of Rinzai Zen, Kyoto is the best place in Japan to try zazen, the seated meditation at the heart of Zen practice. A number of temples run sessions open to visitors, some in English, in which a monk guides you in the posture, breathing and stillness of zazen in a quiet hall, often followed by a short dharma talk and a bowl of tea. In the traditional style, an attendant may walk the hall with the keisaku, a flat wooden stick used to strike the shoulders — not as punishment but, on request, to restore focus.

item.title: Nada Sake Blending Workshop: Make Your Own Bottle — Guide
item.description: Blending — deciding how different tanks are combined into the final product — is one of the quiet arts of sake brewing, and a few Nada breweries now let visitors try it. You are given a set of base sakes that differ in rice variety, yeast, polishing ratio and age, a measuring cylinder and a tasting glass, and talked through how each component behaves: one contributing aroma, another body, another acidity or a dry finish.

item.title: Okinawa Karate Guide: The Birthplace, Dojos & Experiences
item.description: Okinawa is the birthplace of karate, which grew from the indigenous Ryukyu fighting art “te” blended with Chinese martial influences. For practitioners worldwide, training in Okinawa is a pilgrimage to the source; for travellers, it’s a rare chance to step into a traditional dojo and learn the basics — stances, blocks, strikes and the spirit of respect at the heart of the art. With beginner-friendly experiences and the impressive Okinawa Karate Kaikan, anyone can connect with this living heritage.

item.title: Osaka Kendo Class Guide: Try the Way of the Sword
item.description: Behind the thunderous shouts and clashing bamboo of a dojo lies kendo — “the way of the sword,” the modern martial art descended from samurai swordsmanship. A kendo experience class in Osaka lets visitors step onto the dojo floor, grip the bamboo shinai, learn a few basic cuts and stances, and even try on a piece of the armour, all under an instructor who explains the discipline, spirit, and etiquette behind it.

item.title: Osaka Takoyaki Cooking Class Guide: Flip Your Own Octopus Balls
item.description: Eating takoyaki in Osaka is essential — but making it is a different kind of fun. The mesmerising flick-and-turn that shapes runny batter into perfect crisp spheres is genuinely tricky, and a takoyaki-making class lets you try it yourself on a real dimpled pan, with a local teacher guiding your wrist. It’s hands-on, hilarious, and you eat your wonky-but-delicious results at the end — one of Osaka’s most enjoyable and very on-brand experiences for foodies, couples, and families.

item.title: Tokyo Ramen Cooking Class Guide: Make Your Own Bowl from Scratch
item.description: You can eat extraordinary ramen all over Tokyo — but learning to make it transforms how you understand Japan’s most beloved comfort food. A ramen cooking class takes you behind the steaming counter: building a broth, understanding the four components that define every bowl, hand-preparing the toppings, and finally assembling — and eating — a bowl of ramen you made yourself. It’s hands-on, delicious, conducted in English, and one of the most rewarding food experiences in the city, especially for travellers who want to take a real skill home.

item.title: Tokyo Sushi Making Class Guide: Learn from a Trained Itamae
item.description: Sushi looks deceptively simple — a slice of fish on a mound of rice — but every element conceals years of craft. In a Tokyo sushi-making class, a trained itamae (sushi chef) reveals those secrets: how to season and handle the rice, how to wield a Japanese knife, and how to shape nigiri and roll maki with the right pressure and form. You leave not only having eaten beautiful sushi you made yourself, but with knife and rice fundamentals that quietly change how you eat — and make — sushi for the rest of your life.

item.title: Hiroshima Mystery & Escape Rooms: Real-Life Puzzle Adventures
item.description: Japan invented the modern “real-life escape game” — known here as Real Escape Game (リアル脱出ゲーム) — and the format has matured into a national pastime with dozens of operators producing increasingly elaborate puzzle experiences. Hiroshima’s scene is smaller than Tokyo’s or Osaka’s but offers a satisfying mix of permanent escape room venues, walking mystery tours, and history-themed puzzle experiences specific to the prefecture. This guide covers what’s actually available for overseas visitors, including English-friendly options.
